data.title: Which methionine sensor, if either, carries the benefit of methionine restriction?
data.gap: The amino-acid sensors are among the most pathway-specific upstream control points and among the least phenotype-tested; how readily each can be drugged has not been compared systematically. Methionine is now known to be read by two separate sensors, which is why this card asks about a division rather than a single route: SAMTOR binds the metabolite SAM and signals through GATOR1/KICSTOR (GU2017), while PKM2 binds free methionine itself, through a dedicated recognition pocket independent of its glycolytic activity, and signals through GATOR2 (SANG2026, human-cell chemoproteomics with a photoaffinity methionine probe). Those are two different molecules read at two different entry points, so a sensor-attribution question about methionine restriction now has at least two candidate arms, plus the possibility that neither carries the dietary effect. One organismal exception exists in this corpus: LEE2010 (Science 2010) showed that loss of Drosophila Sestrin produces fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle degeneration and cardiac malfunction, all prevented by inhibiting TOR or activating AMPK. That is an organismal age-related-pathology phenotype (A - animal), though not a lifespan endpoint, and it is carried in the pathway model as the SESN2-AGING edge. Beyond that single fly result, the sensors (Sestrin2, CASTOR1, SAMTOR, PKM2, v-ATPase) rest on M - molecular - work only, and no mammalian lifespan and no human ageing endpoint shows that manipulating ONE sensor arm reproduces the benefit of broader mTORC1 inhibition. Read the gap as a mechanism-attribution gap, not as an absence of mammalian data on the nutrients themselves. Dietary methionine restriction does extend mouse lifespan and does improve glucose and insulin measures (Miller 2005 and later work; outside this corpus, which is why no SID is cited here). What has not been shown is the SENSOR claim - that such a benefit is transmitted through SAMTOR to GATOR1, or through PKM2 to GATOR2, or through Sestrin2, rather than through any other consequence of eating less methionine.
data.gap_beginner: The amino-acid sensors in this pathway (Sestrin2, CASTOR1, SAMTOR, PKM2, the lysosome's acid pump) are among the most pathway-specific control points in it - and among the least tested for whether changing them actually changes health or lifespan. Methionine turns out to have two sensors, not one: SAMTOR notices a molecule the cell makes FROM methionine, while PKM2 grabs methionine itself, and each passes the message on by a different handle. So if a low-methionine diet helps, there are now two candidate messengers to blame, and the possibility that neither of them is responsible. There is one organism-level exception: in fruit flies, losing Sestrin caused fat build-up, mitochondrial problems, muscle degeneration and heart trouble, all preventable by turning TOR down. In mammals, the diet side of this does work - feeding mice less methionine makes them live longer and handle blood sugar better. What no study held in this Atlas shows is that the benefit actually travels THROUGH one of these sensors, and none of the sensor routes has been tested that way in people in anything the Atlas holds. That is what this corpus contains as of its snapshot date, which is not the same as saying no such study exists anywhere. So the question is not 'is there any evidence' - it is which of the two sensor routes, if either, carries the effect.
data.changed_since_written: The premise has been disfavoured since 2018, outside this corpus. Methionine restriction delivers its metabolic benefit even in mice with constitutively active hepatic mTORC1, so suppressing mTORC1 is not required for it (Yu and Lamming, FASEB J 2018, PMID 29401631). Its known mediators are hepatic FGF21, the transsulfuration/H2S route (Hine, Cell 2014, PMID 25542313) and separable downstream arms (Wanders, FASEB J 2015, PMID 25742717) — and an H2S donor on its own did not extend lifespan in the ITP (Harrison, GeroScience 2023, PMID 38041783). Separately, the destination this question aims at was already reached genetically without any sensor: reduced mTORC1 alone extended life with normal glucose tolerance in female mTOR/mLST8 double-heterozygous mice (Lamming, Science 2012, PMID 22461615).
data.still_open: What fraction, if any, of methionine restriction's benefit runs through each of the two known sensor arms - SAM to SAMTOR to GATOR1/KICSTOR, and free methionine to PKM2 to GATOR2 - and whether their relative weight differs by tissue or physiological state. Both halves are genuinely untested: no SAMTOR knockout ageing study, no PKM2 methionine-pocket mutant in vivo, and no mammalian Sestrin lifespan study exists in the literature searched. It is now a question about dividing a contribution between two identified routes, not about an unexplored route to geroprotection.
data.hypothesis: Framed as a partition between two sensor arms, not as a single null. Methionine reaches mTORC1 through at least two distinct recognition events: free methionine bound by PKM2, relayed through GATOR2 (SANG2026), and the metabolite SAM bound by SAMTOR, relayed through GATOR1/KICSTOR (GU2017). The testable form has two halves. (1) If methionine restriction's healthspan effects persist unchanged in a SAMTOR-null or SAM-binding-dead knock-in mouse, the SAMTOR arm is not what carries that particular dietary benefit. (2) If they also persist in a mouse whose PKM2 methionine-binding pocket is disabled without touching its glycolytic activity, neither sensor arm carries it, and the benefit runs through some other consequence of eating less methionine. Either result would show the sensor dispensable for transmitting the diet; neither would show that drugging the sensor has no geroprotective value, which is a separate experiment. Whether the two arms are redundant, additive, or split by tissue is itself untested.
data.hypothesis_beginner: Turned around into a form that can fail, for two sensors rather than one: if mice engineered without a working SAM sensor still get the full benefit of a low-methionine diet, that sensor is not how the benefit travels - and if mice whose free-methionine sensor is also disabled still get it, neither sensor is. Each result argues against that particular route; on its own, neither result would show that a drug aimed at the sensor could never help, which is a different test.
data.how_to_test: Two arms, tested separately and then together. (1) SAMTOR-null or SAM-binding-dead knock-in mice on methionine-restricted against control diet; healthspan, glucose tolerance and mTORC2 activity as endpoints. (2) A PKM2 knock-in that disables the methionine-recognition pocket while leaving enzymatic activity intact - the separation SANG2026 reports in cells, which is what makes a clean genetic test possible - on the same diets. (3) Both together, to ask whether the arms are redundant. One confound to design around: Sestrin loss is deleterious rather than geroprotective - it abolishes the benefits of exercise, acting through AKT and PGC1-alpha (Kim, Nat Commun 2020, PMID 31929512) - so a Sestrin knockout does not test this hypothesis. A second: PKM2 is a glycolytic enzyme, so any whole-body knockout confounds the sensing question with metabolic effects; the binding-pocket mutant is the point. Secondary and cheaper: does hepatic PRMT1 inhibition, which improved insulin sensitivity in aged mice (Jiang, Cell Metab 2023, PMID 38006878), reproduce the metabolic half without mTORC2 loss?
revision_log: 2026-08-30: The evidence basis previously read 'supported ONLY by tier-D mechanistic studies and links to ZERO aging/longevity outcomes'. That was already false when displayed: LEE2010 had been added after the July 2026 external review, but this card had not been updated.
2026-09-21: Scope clarified as a mechanism-attribution gap. An earlier beginner-register version said 'nothing equivalent has been shown in a mammal', which overstated the gap.

2026-09-29: 'the most pharmacologically specific nodes' and 'most precise, most drug-friendly' softened, because no comparative analysis supports them. The Lamming 2012 result is now qualified as female mice.

2026-10-03: SANG2026 added - human-cell chemoproteomics identifying PKM2 as a methionine sensor acting through GATOR2 to mTORC1, complementing the SAMTOR/GATOR1 arm but not addressing the ageing contribution.

2026-11-06: The card was still formulated almost entirely as a question about SAMTOR's contribution, although SANG2026 had been linked here since 2026-10-03 and PKM2 and its two edges (MET-PKM2, PKM2-GATOR2) were already in the pathway model. Rewritten as a partition between two identified sensor arms - free methionine to PKM2 to GATOR2, and SAM to SAMTOR to GATOR1/KICSTOR - with the possibility that neither carries the dietary effect kept open. The proposed experiment gained a second arm (a PKM2 knock-in that disables the methionine-recognition pocket while leaving glycolytic activity intact, which is the separation SANG2026 reports in cells) and a warning that a whole-body PKM2 knockout confounds sensing with metabolism. Title changed from 'Sensor-selective geroprotection without the metabolic penalty' to a question; URL locked to the old slug via URL_Slug so /question/ addresses do not break.

2026-11-07: External audit, point on absence claims. The beginner text said that nobody has shown the benefit travelling through a sensor and that no human study has tested it at all. Both were unbounded claims about the whole field made from the contents of this corpus. They are now scoped to what the Atlas holds at its snapshot date, with a sentence saying that this is not the same as no such study existing anywhere. The expert text was already scoped and is unchanged.
